claims.text: Local lattice distortions are the primary factor governing strength and deformation behavior in multi-component concentrated alloys.
Local lattice distortions impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion caused by lattice distortion increases yield strength.
Changing the magnitude of lattice distortion alters strain-hardening behavior.
The initial material is a single-phase concentrated alloy with a uniform but highly distorted lattice.
Selecting alloying elements with more similar atomic radii will decrease lattice distortion.
Phase stability can be kept approximately constant while alloying elements are changed to reduce lattice distortion.
Dislocation climb and diffusional processes are minimized at the proposed room-to-moderately-elevated testing temperatures.
The magnitude of local lattice distortion can be quantified using X-ray diffraction peak broadening or atomic-scale TEM imaging.
Local lattice distortions create a spatially variable energy landscape.
The variable energy landscape increases friction stress against dislocation motion.
The high-distortion baseline alloy will have higher yield strength than the reduced-distortion variant.
The high-distortion baseline and reduced-distortion variant will exhibit different strain-hardening rates.
The proposed lattice-distortion mechanism should dominate when thermal activation does not significantly enable climb or diffusion.
The proposed mechanism may not govern behavior in alloys containing significant secondary phases.
Chemical short-range order may also influence the observed mechanical behavior.
Failure to observe a statistically significant reduction in yield strength and a change in strain hardening after reducing lattice distortion would falsify the hypothesis.
